original_value: We estimate the effect of supply chain proximity on product quality. Merging four automotive data sets, we create a supply chain sample that reports the failure rate of 27,807 auto components, the location of 529 upstream component factories, and the location of 275 downstream assembly plants. We find that defect rates are higher when upstream and downstream factories are farther apart. Specifically, we estimate that increasing the distance between an upstream component factory and a downstream assembly plant by an order of magnitude increases the component’s expected defect rate by 3.9%. We find that quality improves more slowly across geographically dispersed supply chains. We also find that supply chain distance is more detrimental to quality when automakers produce early-generation models or high-end products, when they buy components with more complex configurations, or when they source from suppliers who invest relatively little in research and development.This paper was accepted by Vishal Gaur, operations management.

result.paraphrase: We estimate how supply-chain proximity affects product quality. By combining four automotive datasets, we build a supply-chain sample that records failure rates for 27,807 auto components along with the locations of 529 upstream component factories and 275 downstream assembly plants. Our results show that defect rates rise as upstream and downstream factories are located farther apart. In particular, we estimate that a tenfold increase in the distance between an upstream component factory and a downstream assembly plant raises the component’s expected defect rate by 3.9%. Quality therefore improves more slowly in geographically dispersed supply chains. We also find that supply-chain distance hurts quality more when automakers make early-generation models or high-end products, when they purchase components with more complex configurations, or when they source from suppliers that invest relatively little in research and development. This paper was accepted by Vishal Gaur, operations management.
